Path to Profitability — The Integration Tax
Diginex's profitability trajectory hinges on a classic M&A math problem: near-term margin compression from integration costs, offset by longer-term operating leverage as the unified platform scales.

Market Cap
The near-term headwind
The company is in active integration mode across four acquisitions.
In H1 FY25 (six months to September 2025), general and administrative expenses climbed $3.4M to $8.1M, with $2.2M of that driven by M&A due diligence and legal work.
That's roughly 27% of the G&A increase attributable to one-time integration costs — meaningful, but not catastrophic.

The Resulticks acquisition ($1.5B) is the largest and most complex, adding a separate AI-driven customer data platform that will require significant systems integration, sales alignment, and product consolidation work.
This will likely extend the integration tax into 2027 and beyond.
The path forward
Profitability depends on three things happening in sequence:
Revenue scaling faster than G&A growth.
If Diginex can grow top-line revenue 30–50% YoY while holding G&A flat or growing single digits (as integration work tapers), operating leverage kicks in.
The platform thesis only works if the combined entity has stronger unit economics than the sum of its parts.
Resulticks cross-sell traction.
The $1.5B bet only justifies itself if existing Diginex customers adopt Resulticks' capabilities, and vice versa.
Without cross-sell, you have two siloed businesses with duplicate overhead — a value trap, not a platform.
Geographic expansion momentum.
Diginex has signalled focus on Brazil's $77B sustainability market.
If that expansion gains traction, it provides a new revenue stream that can absorb fixed costs more efficiently than the core business alone.
The realism check
At a $34M market cap and negative earnings, Diginex is priced for execution risk.
The stock has already priced in significant scepticism — meaning a credible path to profitability (even 18–24 months out) could re-rate the stock sharply.
Conversely, any sign that integration is slowing revenue growth or that cross-sell is weaker than expected would likely drive further downside.
The company needs to show in its next 2–3 earnings reports that revenue is accelerating and G&A is decelerating relative to revenue growth.
Until then, profitability remains a narrative, not a fact.
